title: Bloody Tears Came with a Young Teen's Periods, and Doctors Suspect Endometriosis Near Her Eyes
text:
Bloody Tears Came with a Young Teen's Periods, and Doctors Suspect Endometriosis Near Her Eyes
A girl in her early teens began shedding blood-tinged tears, and the episodes kept arriving on the same schedule as her menstrual periods. Eye exams, a battery of blood tests, and an MRI of her eye sockets all came back normal, so her doctors in Istanbul landed on an explanation few would think of first: endometriosis somewhere around the eye.
Gynecologists at Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University School of Medicine and Acıbadem Atakent University described the case on October 12, 2026, in the Journal of Surgical Case Reports. After two years of hormone therapy, her pain and eye bleeding had dropped sharply. The diagnosis, however, was never confirmed with a tissue sample.
Blood at the Corner of Her Eye, Right on Schedule
The girl came to the clinic with cyclical bleeding from the eye that lined up with menstruation, a phenomenon doctors call catamenial hemolacria. She also had pain in her groin, around her eyes, on her lips, and near her navel.
She had started menstruating about a year earlier, and her cycles had never been regular. She had no chronic illnesses, took no regular medications, and had never had surgery. She brought photos and video of the episodes, and one image in the report shows blood droplets pooled at the inner corner of her left eye.
Her abdominal exam was normal. A pelvic ultrasound showed a uterus of normal size and healthy-looking ovaries, with no masses or fluid.
A Search That Turned Up Nothing
Bloody tears can signal serious problems, so the team sent her to eye and blood specialists. Known causes include infections, swollen tear sacs, abnormal blood vessels, bleeding disorders and tumors. A 2023 review in the journal Eye asked outright whether blood-stained tears are a red flag for cancer.
Each concern was ruled out. A complete blood count, clotting tests, von Willebrand factor, platelet function assays, a thrombophilia panel and iron studies were all normal. A detailed eye exam, including microscope views of the front and back of the eye and vision testing, found nothing. An orbital MRI, ordered to look for problems in the tear drainage system or tangled blood vessels, showed no structural lesions.
With every test clean and the bleeding tied tightly to her cycle, the doctors made a presumptive diagnosis of ocular endometriosis.
Endometriosis Beyond the Pelvis Is Hard to Prove
Endometriosis is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows elsewhere in the body. The authors note that it affects roughly 10% of women of reproductive age. It usually involves the ovaries and pelvic lining, but it also turns up, less often, in the bowel and urinary tract. Eye involvement, the authors write, is exceptionally rare.
How such tissue could end up near the eye is not known. Proposed routes for endometriosis outside the pelvis include backward menstrual flow, spread through the blood or lymph system, transformation of other cells, and hormone-driven inflammation.
Proving it is the hard part. The NIH's Child Health Institute says surgery is currently the only way to confirm endometriosis, and the authors explain that sampling tissue from around the eye is often not feasible. Instead, they leaned on the timing of her symptoms, the exclusion of other causes, and her response to treatment. A 2023 review of eyes, menstruation and endometriosis described the same diagnostic bind.
Similar cases have surfaced before. A 2023 report described ocular vicarious menstruation, cyclical eye bleeding during periods, as a rare cause of repeated bleeding on the white of the eye. In 2021, clinicians in India reported a 25-year-old woman who wept blood from both eyes during two periods and had no further episodes on birth control pills at a three-month checkup. The new case adds an adolescent patient, pain in several spots on her body, and two years of follow-up.
Two Years of Hormone Therapy, With Some Bleeding Left
Doctors started her on dienogest, a progestin, at 2 milligrams a day, along with a combined birth control pill containing 0.03 milligrams of ethinyl estradiol. At two years, she reported minimal menstrual pain and far fewer eye bleeding episodes.
The treatment did not erase the problem. Small amounts of bloody tearing still appeared during some cycles. Her regimen was later switched to dienogest combined with estradiol valerate, which her doctors plan to continue until she wants to conceive. The eye and blood specialists did not recommend further follow-up.
The report has clear limits. It describes one patient, and without tissue confirmation, endometriosis remains a well-reasoned hypothesis rather than a proven cause. Hormone therapy suppresses the menstrual cycle broadly, so her improvement fits the theory but cannot by itself pin down the mechanism.
The authors also used the case to flag a wider problem: endometriosis in teenagers is often missed because painful periods and pelvic pain get dismissed as normal. Blood in the tears, in a child or an adult, should be checked by a doctor, since some causes need prompt treatment.
Key Questions Answered
What happened to the patient?
A girl in her early teens had recurring bloody tears and eye pain that coincided with her menstrual periods.
What is hemolacria?
It is the medical term for tears that contain blood. Possible causes include infections, tear sac problems, abnormal blood vessels, bleeding disorders, and tumors, so it warrants a medical evaluation.
Why did doctors suspect endometriosis?
Her bleeding followed her menstrual cycle, other causes were ruled out, and her symptoms improved on hormone therapy.
Was the diagnosis confirmed?
No. Tissue sampling from around the eye is often not feasible, so the diagnosis remains presumptive.
How was she treated?
With dienogest and a combined birth control pill, later switched to dienogest with estradiol valerate.
Did the bleeding stop completely?
Not entirely. Episodes became much less frequent over two years, but minor bloody tearing still appeared during some cycles.
